item.title: How does community of inquiry matter? Mediating effects and configurational pathways linking project-based learning design to learning engagement
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AIGC) has reshaped animation students’ skill profiles and the conditions of instructional design in project-based learning (PBL) studios. We examine whether and how perceptions of PBL design are associated with Learning Engagement (LE), treating AIGC-assisted PBL studios as the research context rather than testing generative AI as a model variable. Drawing on Community of Inquiry (CoI) theory, we examine Problem Driven (PD), Project Design (PDe), Project Implementation (PI), and Project Evaluation (PE) as antecedents; Cognitive Presence (CP), Social Presence (SP), and Teaching Presence (TP) as statistical mediators; and LE as the outcome. We analyzed two-wave survey data from 490 upper-year animation students using PLS-SEM and fsQCA. PBL and CoI were measured concurrently at T1, and LE at T2; indirect effects therefore represent indirect statistical associations rather than mediation with a fully established temporal sequence. PD, PDe, and PI showed significant positive direct associations with LE. PE’s zero-order and single-predictor associations were positive, but its direct path coefficient became significantly negative after controlling for the other PBL dimensions and CoI mediators. The coefficient was sensitive to model specification, suggesting possible statistical suppression; it should not be interpreted as evidence that evaluation itself inherently inhibits engagement. The three CoI dimensions showed significant statistical mediation associations across all 12 indirect paths. TP and SP had relatively higher point estimates of indirect statistical associations, but differences between indirect effects were not formally tested; no dimension is claimed to be optimal. PE’s positive indirect associations through CoI partially offset its negative net direct association without reversing the total association after adjustment. The extent of this offset may depend on the degree to which CoI-related experiences are concurrently reported. fsQCA identified seven high-engagement configurations. No individual PBL dimension was indispensable. CoI dimensions appeared as core or peripheral conditions, although not every configuration included all three. These findings clarify the dual pathways linking evaluation and engagement through indirect statistical associations and configurational conditions, and provide guidance for optimizing PBL under different resource constraints. Conclusions are limited to AIGC-assisted PBL studios and do not establish the instructional effects of generative AI.

item.title: Psychological mechanisms of perceived technological dependence on generative artificial intelligence tools: perceived knowledge, trust, anxiety, and self-efficacy
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative AI tools are increasingly used in design education, yet the relationship between students’ perceptions of these tools and their reported reliance on them remains unclear. This study analyzed cross-sectional survey responses from 526 undergraduate students in design-related disciplines using partial least squares structural equation modeling. In the specified model, perceived reliability, perceived usefulness, and perceived intelligence were positively associated with perceived AIGC knowledge, whereas perceived ease of use was not significantly associated with it. Perceived AIGC knowledge was positively associated with trust, self-efficacy, and usage intention and negatively associated with AIGC-related anxiety. Trust, AIGC-related anxiety, and self-efficacy each showed a significant indirect effect in the modeled relationship between perceived AIGC knowledge and usage intention. Usage intention was strongly associated with perceived technological dependence. These findings are consistent with the proposed framework, but the cross-sectional data do not establish the temporal sequence of the constructs or show that reported dependence reflects harmful overuse. The study extends technology acceptance research by examining perceived reliance in AIGC-supported creative work.

item.title: If it doesn’t have a soul, it doesn’t hurt? The effect of bullying and social anxiety on the use of conversational AI
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) increasingly functions as a social interaction partner, raising questions about how established interpersonal behaviors transfer to human-AI interaction. The present study examined whether bullying-like behavior directed toward CAI reflects the extension of real world social strategies, and how social anxiety, prior bullying experiences, and AI self-competency contribute to such behavior. Methods Participants ( N = 289) completed measures of social anxiety, prior bullying perpetration and victimization, AI self-competency, and bullying-like behavior directed toward conversational AI. Results Through several analyses, bully-victims exhibited the highest levels of AI-directed bullying-like behavior. The interaction between bullying perpetration and victimization emerged as the strongest predictor in our regression analysis, while prior bullying perpetration alone was not sufficient to explain AI-directed aggression, and prior victimization alone was negatively associated with AI-directed bullying-like behavior. Social anxiety did not directly predict bullying-like behavior toward AI; however, mediation analyses showed that prior victimization fully mediated the relationship between social anxiety and bullying-like behavior towards CAI. Individuals with higher social anxiety were more likely to report victimization, which in turn was associated with increased bullying-like behavior toward AI. AI self-competency did not emerge as an independent predictor. Discussion These findings suggest that AI-directed bullying-like behavior is best understood as a context-dependent behavior arising from the co-occurrence of aggression and vulnerability, rather than a direct extension of general aggressive tendencies. Conversational AI constitutes a distinct relational context that can both reflect and reinforce existing behavioral patterns. This has important implications for understanding how human-AI interactions may shape social behavior and psychological functioning over time.

item.title: Artificial intelligence-generated and algorithmically personalized music interventions and their effects on brain function, behavior, and health: a critical review
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
This critical review synthesizes empirical studies of algorithmically personalized and artificial-intelligence-generated music interventions reporting neurophysiological, neuroimaging, or objective behavioral outcomes. Literature was identified through structured searches of PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and the ACM Digital Library through 12 August 2026, with CNKI and Wanfang searched on 22 September 2026, supplemented by citation tracking. Twenty-one eligible studies (at least 1,005 participants) were identified. Five things the term artificial intelligence covers in this literature are separated: algorithmic selection from a corpus, rule-based sonification, parametric modulation of pre-existing material, machine-learning generative composition, and closed-loop delivery contingent on the listener’s own signal. Only three studies used a machine-learning generative model, so most of the evidence concerns algorithmic personalization of existing material. Studies of closed-loop neural systems reported the most consistent neurophysiological signal, and music-based alpha neurofeedback produced higher normalized alpha power than yoked random feedback. In an open-loop design, personalized EEG-derived music was reported to attenuate anxiety induction where self-selected preferred music and silence did not, with enhanced prefrontal theta oscillations as the associated correlate. Eight studies carried a comparator capable of isolating an algorithmic component from music exposure, and all eight favored the algorithmic condition. These eight address different causal questions, use different designs, and point to no single mechanism, so their results are best read as preliminary and hypothesis-generating. Evidence quality was very low throughout. The median reported sample size was 22, no study blinded participants or measured expectancy, and no specific finding has been independently replicated. GRADE certainty was very low for every outcome domain, covering EEG oscillatory power, sleep architecture, autonomic regulation, epileptiform activity, and cognitive, behavioral and affective outcomes. Neurophysiological change is reported more often than behavioral change, and behavioral change more often than clinical benefit. The evidence supports continued investigation and does not support clinical deployment. Eight reporting and design requirements for future trials are proposed.

item.title: Human or Algorithmic Managers in Expert Knowledge Work? The Interplay of Management Style and Managerial Function
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Algorithmic management is entering expert knowledge work, but when workers accept algorithmic rather than human managers remains unclear. We surveyed Finnish expert knowledge workers (N = 1,156) using a factorial scenario experiment varying manager type (human/algorithmic), management style (controlling/balanced /flexible), and six managerial functions and measured leader–member exchange (LMX), organizational trust, AI familiarity and work complexity. Findings cover five functions; rewarding was excluded due to insufficient model fit. Management style was the strongest predictor: flexible styles were rated highest and controlling lowest, regardless of manager type. Human managers were preferred for goal setting, performance evaluation, and supportive leadership; algorithms only for scheduling under controlling conditions. Monitoring showed no consistent difference. High-quality LMX buffered reactions to controlling styles, and in performance evaluation and supportive leadership its association with acceptability was stronger for algorithmic managers, narrowing the human advantage. Organizational trust and LMX were more consistently implicated than AI familiarity, qualifying algorithm-aversion accounts.

item.title: How Large Language Models Weight Narrative Cues When Detecting Deception in Oral Accounts: A Multi‐Model Comparison
item.description:
Applied Cognitive Psychology
ABSTRACT Lie detection research has increasingly turned to artificial intelligence, yet the application of large language models (LLMs) remains underexplored for transcribed oral narratives. We compared five LLMs (Gemini‐3‐flash, Gemini‐3‐pro, Deepseek‐v4‐flash, GPT‐5.6‐luna, and Grok‐4) in classifying truthful and deceptive statements from interview transcripts of oral travel narratives collected from 95 Chinese‐speaking participants. Guided by Criteria‐Based Content Analysis (CBCA), Reality Monitoring (RM), and the Verifiability Approach (VA), theory‐driven prompts instructed models to score five narrative cues before making binary veracity judgments. Gemini‐3‐flash achieved the highest accuracy (74.74%, AUC = 0.76) with 81.63% sensitivity and 67.39% specificity, and stable repeated‐run performance. For this optimal model, unusual/superfluous details served as the sole significant predictor of objective veracity even after controlling for text length. LLMs can detect deception above chance but show large performance heterogeneity. Independent human coding, cross‐cultural replications, and adversarial robustness testing are needed before real‐world deployment.

item.title: “What Am I Really Doing with My Own Brain?”: College Students on Learning, Ownership, and AI
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
Generative artificial intelligence gives college students new ways to support their learning, while also raising questions about what they still want to learn and do for themselves. This qualitative study draws on semi-structured interviews with 14 undergraduates at a Northeastern liberal arts college to examine how students distinguish between AI use that supports their own thinking and AI use that substitutes for it, what they believe is worth doing on their own, and whether and how purpose enters their reasoning about learning and AI use. Using the Framework Method with a cross-case matrix to compare patterns across participants and topics, we found that students repeatedly drew a line between using AI as a supportive tool and letting it take the place of their own thinking or authorship. Students most often talked about wanting to keep developing their own skills, thinking independently, and knowing what they could actually do without AI. They also wanted the work to still feel “like theirs,” citing ownership, pride, authenticity, and ethical concerns. Students also described pressures that made AI appealing, including heavy workloads, deadlines, grades, convenience, and concerns about falling behind their peers. Although few participants explicitly connected their AI choices to a stated purpose, many described concerns that may be relevant to purpose development, including developing valued skills and strengths, acting on personal values, and becoming the kind of person they hoped to be. We consider these concerns through a purpose-mindset framework while distinguishing our interpretation from participants’ own explanations of their AI choices. The findings suggest that understanding students’ AI use requires attention to what they believe they need to learn and do for themselves.

item.title: When college students perceive GAI feedback as credible: the role of perceived GAI feedback credibility in promoting deep learning through cognitive engagement
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has rapidly developed in higher education and has raised new questions from an educational psychology perspective. Why does GAI feedback promote meaningful learning for some college students but fail to produce similar learning benefits for others? To answer this question, this study develops a theoretical framework based on Information Processing Theory, Elaboration Likelihood Model, and Constructivist Learning Theory. This study examines how perceived GAI feedback credibility influences college students’ deep learning and explores the mediating role of cognitive engagement in this relationship. This study adopts a stratified simple sampling method and collects questionnaire data from 506 undergraduate students and uses structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the proposed model. The results show that perceived GAI feedback credibility has positive relationships with both cognitive engagement and deep learning. In addition, cognitive engagement plays a significant mediating role between perceived GAI feedback credibility and deep learning, suggesting that credible GAI feedback may support deep learning by encouraging college students to engage in cognitive processing and reflective thinking. This study extends research on learning psychology in GAI-supported learning environments by explaining how college students evaluate and process GAI feedback. The findings indicate that the influence of GAI feedback on learning does not simply result from the technology itself. Instead, college students’ judgments of feedback credibility and their following cognitive engagement play important roles in shaping deep learning processes.

item.title: Clinical characteristics, semiology, and comorbidity patterns in non-epileptic seizures (NES): a retrospective comparative study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Objectives Non-epileptic seizures (NES) are paroxysmal events resembling epileptic seizures but not explained by ictal activity. Differential diagnosis may be challenging, particularly because NES and epilepsy can coexist. We aimed to characterize the demographic, clinical, semiological, psychiatric, and instrumental profile of patients with NES, compare patients with NES only with patients with NES epilepsy-only, and assess the robustness of the main associations through sensitivity analyses. Methods We conducted a retrospective observational comparative study using a clinical database from our Neurology Unit (2022–2025) including 38 patients with NES and 23 patients with epilepsy without NES. A total of 18 NES patients had comorbid epilepsy; therefore, the primary comparison included mutually exclusive groups: NES-only ( n = 20) and epilepsy-only ( n = 23). All NES patients were retained for descriptive analyses. Between-group comparisons used exact or non-parametric tests with Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate (BH-FDR) correction. Sensitivity analyses restricted NES-only patients to those with database-recorded video-EEG confirmation and used Firth penalized logistic regression adjusted for age and sex. Results Among 38 patients with NES, 94.7% had documented psychological/psychiatric comorbidity, mainly anxiety (50.0%) and depression (28.9%). Positive motor phenomena were documented in 73.7%, neurological examination inconsistency/incongruity in 85.7% of evaluable patients, and video-EEG confirmation in 73.7%. Psychological/psychiatric comorbidity was significantly more frequent in NES-only than epilepsy-only patients (90.0% vs. 13.0%; exact OR 50.40, 95% CI 7.29–670.28; BH-FDR p < 0.001), as was anxiety (45.0% vs. 4.3%; BH-FDR p = 0.014). Broad seizure-semiology domains were not significantly different after multiplicity correction. Among imaged patients, abnormal MRI findings were more frequent in epilepsy-only patients (12/18 vs. 0/10; BH-FDR p = 0.006), although MRI ascertainment differed between groups. The psychiatric-comorbidity association persisted in sensitivity analyses. Conclusion NES showed substantial clinical heterogeneity and frequently coexisted with epilepsy. Psychological/psychiatric comorbidity was markedly more frequent in NES-only than epilepsy-only patients and remained robust in sensitivity analyses, although differential ascertainment limits interpretation. Broad seizure manifestations alone did not distinguish the groups after multiplicity correction. Instrumental findings should be considered descriptive rather than NES biomarkers. These findings support explicit stratification for comorbid epilepsy and standardized prospective assessment of psychiatric and semiological features.

item.title: AI literacy is directly associated with positive attitudes and indirectly associated with negative attitudes through AI anxiety: a cross-sectional study of preservice teachers
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Positive and negative attitudes toward artificial intelligence (AI) may have partly distinct psychological correlates. This cross-sectional study examined whether AI anxiety statistically accounted for associations between AI literacy and positive and negative attitudes toward AI among preservice teachers. Methods Participants were 335 preservice teachers enrolled in a faculty of education in Türkiye. Data were collected using the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale, Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale, and a personal information form. Two indirect-effect models were estimated using PROCESS Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, controlling for prior AI training. Results AI literacy was negatively associated with AI anxiety and positively associated with positive attitudes toward AI. AI anxiety was positively associated with negative attitudes but was not significantly associated with positive attitudes. The indirect association through AI anxiety was significant for negative attitudes but not for positive attitudes, and a direct bootstrap contrast confirmed that the two indirect effects differed significantly (B = −0.118, 95% CI [−0.201, −0.039]). Prior AI training was not significantly associated with either attitude dimension. A sensitivity analysis excluding the three reverse-worded AI literacy items reproduced this pattern. Discussion The findings indicate that positive and negative attitudes toward AI may have partly distinct psychological correlates: AI literacy is directly related to positive evaluations, whereas its association with negative evaluations is statistically linked to AI anxiety. Because the data are cross-sectional, the indirect effects should not be interpreted as evidence of causal mediation.

item.title: Within-person reciprocal processes between AI feedback literacy and agentic engagement: a three-wave random-intercept cross-lagged panel study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Artificial intelligence (AI) feedback has become a pervasive feature of university learning, yet whether students’ capacity to engage productively with such feedback co-develops with their broader learner agency remains poorly understood. Drawing on student feedback literacy theory, self-determination theory as a supplementary motivational lens, and the mutualism principle, this study tested whether AI feedback literacy and agentic engagement reciprocally predict each other over time at the within-person level and exploratorily examined whether they share a stable trait-level association. A three-wave panel study of 480 Chinese undergraduates ( N = 399 with complete data across all waves), with measurements at six-week intervals across one semester, was analyzed using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM). At the between-person level, students who scored systematically higher in AI feedback literacy across the semester also scored systematically higher in agentic engagement, with a moderate and statistically significant trait-level correlation between the two random intercepts ( r = 0.315, p < 0.001), supporting Hypothesis 1. At the within-person level, both cross-lagged pathways were positive and significant: deviations in AI feedback literacy predicted later deviations in agentic engagement ( β = 0.222, p < 0.001), and the reverse pathway was likewise significant ( β = 0.263, p < 0.001). A Wald test indicated that the two reciprocal pathways did not differ significantly in magnitude (Δ B = 0.002, p = 0.972), consistent with a symmetric mutualism. A model comparison confirmed that the RI-CLPM provided substantially better fit than a traditional cross-lagged panel model, with the RI-CLPM revealing substantially larger within-person reciprocal effects once stable trait-level covariation was properly isolated. The findings extend the mutualism principle from a coupling of person-internal constructs to a coupling between a person-internal competency and a person-environment behavioral interface. They also raise the possibility, in a Confucian Heritage Culture context where agentic engagement has historically been culturally muted, that AI feedback may offer a less culturally-loaded venue in which students can exercise agency. The study repositions AI feedback literacy from a static skill into a dynamic developmental resource that is constituted, in part, by the very engagement it enables.

item.title: CEP-MI: a novel cue-execution dual-stage motor imagery paradigm with PGCANet decoding architecture
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Background Motor imagery-based brain-computer interface (MI-BCI) holds great potential in neurorehabilitation and motor assistance. Data quality and motor intention decoding effectiveness are closely associated with participants’ engagement. However, previous MI tasks ignored active engagement regulation, and neural mechanisms underlying the transition from motor imagery to execution remain unclear, with limited relevant research. Conventional separate-trial designs cannot capture continuous brain dynamics from imagery to execution and cannot objectively evaluate subject engagement, which hinders mechanism exploration and stable decoding. Methods To address these paradigm-related limitations, a novel cue-execution MI paradigm (CEP-MI) with countdown anchors was designed to quantify engagement. Motor execution sessions were added post-imagery to reveal neural differences during the transition and identify movement-related brain activities. Meanwhile, to boost MI-EEG decoding performance, a collaborative decoding architecture (PGCANet) integrating prior guidance and channel awareness was proposed, with dual branches and consistency constraint loss for decision fusion. Results CEP-MI effectively quantifies participant engagement, and PGCANet achieves superior decoding performance compared to traditional algorithms and advanced models, with the optimal average accuracy reaching 85.77% in binary classification and 82.47% in quadruple classification. Conclusion Targeting the above-mentioned research gaps, the CEP-MI paradigm provides valuable insights into the imagery-execution transition mechanism. PGCANet enhances MI decoding accuracy via multi-branch collaboration, laying a foundation for MI-BCI’s clinical application in neurorehabilitation. Significance This study introduces a novel paradigm and collaborative architecture that significantly advance MI-BCI decoding accuracy and engagement quantification, and helps to promote its clinical application in neurorehabilitation.

item.title: Effects of question-chain prompting on self-regulated learning, metacognition, and achievement in a generative AI environment
item.description:
International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers learners immediate and personalized support, yet unguided interaction may encourage passive use and weaken self-regulated learning (SRL). This study examined whether question-chain prompting can support SRL in human-AI interaction. A quasi-experiment was conducted with 83 undergraduates enrolled in a television program production course. A control group used free-form questioning, whereas two experimental groups used either a progressive or a divergent question-chain strategy. Data included GenAI interaction logs, post-task reflections, metacognitive awareness measures, and course grades. This study found that both question-chain groups demonstrated significantly more learning-strategy and learning-monitoring behaviors than the control group. Reflection data further indicated differences in students’ approaches to human-AI collaboration, although these differences should be interpreted cautiously because the reflection prompts differed by condition. Moreover, both experimental groups scored significantly higher than the control group on knowledge of cognition, regulation of cognition, and academic achievement. No significant differences were found between the progressive and divergent question-chain approaches. The findings suggest that question-chain prompting, implemented as an instructional package of specific, sequenced, and required questions, can promote more active engagement during human-AI interaction and support metacognitive development and learning performance. Question chains offer a practical approach for guiding students’ use of GenAI in educational settings.

item.title: Beyond good and bad: An in-depth study of student and teacher views on generative AI in high school.
item.description:
Technology Mind and Behavior
Public and scholarly discussions of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education often emphasize sharp divides, portraying students as enthusiastic adopters unconcerned with learning and teachers as reluctant gatekeepers focused on control and assessment.However, little empirical work has examined how students' and teachers' attitudes toward AI are formed, expressed, and negotiated in everyday social contexts.We conducted in-depth interviews with 31 high school students and 29 high school teachers from five states in the United States to quantitatively examine how both groups reason about generative AI tools in education.Participants rarely expressed simple endorsement or rejection of AI; instead, they often articulated tensions between perceived benefits and risks.Students and teachers described AI as useful and engaging but also potentially undermining genuine learning and skill development.Participants also expressed uncertainty about appropriate use, the reliability of AI outputs, and the long-term implications of AI for education.Attitudes toward AI were shaped through ongoing peer interaction, with many participants describing how conversations and shared experiences influenced their views.Together, these findings suggest that attitudes toward generative AI in education are best understood as socially negotiated responses to a rapidly evolving technology rather than in terms of generational divides.More broadly, the findings highlight how integrating AI into education requires ongoing reflection about the role technology should play in learning and human development.

item.title: Shaping early childhood in the age of AI: holistic competencies, pedagogical practices, and ecological support
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the learning and developmental contexts in which young children grow, learn, and interact. Guided by an ecological perspective, this systematic conceptual mapping review examines 86 resources to explore what young children should learn and how they should be taught. Four themes were identified through thematic analysis: (1) holistic competencies for young children, encompassing foundational cognitive and social–emotional skills, physical and mental well-being, executive functions, learning dispositions, and AI literacy; (2) governance for AI integration in early childhood education; (3) professional development and systemic support for educators; and (4) play-based learning and human-centered approaches in AI-enhanced contexts. The findings suggest that thriving in the AI age requires moving beyond isolated digital skills toward holistic development, supported by a cohesive infrastructure that links classroom practice with structural governance. These findings highlight the necessity of cultivating holistic competencies beyond basic AI literacy in curriculum design, preparing children to navigate an ever-changing digital world. Furthermore, they underscore the imperative for robust institutional support, particularly through participatory research to support age-appropriate pedagogy and educators’ digital confidence, while highlighting the value of playful early learning. Concurrently, these insights establish a theoretical framework for future empirical research, offer actionable strategies for ethical child-centred AI implementation, and provide strategic directions for policy and practice to address the critical demand for transformative knowledge in early childhood education.

item.title: Gendered affective representations in AI-assisted music videos: a qualitative multimethod study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become increasingly visible in music-video production, influencing both production practices and the ways in which emotion, bodies, and gender are portrayed visually. This study examines gendered emotional representation in AI-assisted music videos. Methods A qualitative multimethod design combined interpretive visual analysis of four purposively selected AI-assisted music videos with asynchronous written expert interviews involving six creative-industry professionals and four psychology experts ( N = 10). The videos were analysed through an interpretive coding framework covering emotion, gender, body and face, power relations, AI aesthetics, and traces of bias. Results Across the cases, emotion was conveyed not only through facial expression but also through atmosphere, colour, movement, editing, and spatial transitions. The selected works sometimes reproduced familiar conventions, including heteronormative intimacy, militarised masculinity, and idealised female bodies, but also unsettled them through female anger and solidarity and mutable synthetic bodies. Ambiguity in a body’s appearance did not necessarily unsettle its gendered narrative role. Industry accounts described how prompting, selection, revision, and post-production shape representations, while general psychology-expert perspectives informed their interpretation. Discussion The findings position AI-assisted music videos as co-produced sites of synthetic visual culture in which established gendered conventions may be repeated, negotiated, or challenged. Neither expert group provided direct evidence about the production or reception of the selected videos. The findings underline the practical importance of representational review, consent, diversity, and transparent disclosure in AI-assisted cultural production.

item.title: Parasocial and interpersonal interaction: distinct associations with customer value co-creation in virtual brand communities
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Virtual brand communities expose members to communication from the brand side and interaction with other members, but these sources may not relate to participation through the same psychological processes. Drawing on the stimulus organism response framework, social identity theory, and social cognitive theory, this study tested whether community identification and self-efficacy statistically accounted for indirect associations between parasocial interaction, interpersonal interaction, and customer value co-creation behavior. The hypotheses were examined in an unpublished cross-sectional survey of 240 adult users of virtual brand communities in China. An audit of the questionnaire and data codebook corrected a prior item-block parsing error and established the intended 30-item measurement structure. Internal consistency was acceptable for the five composites (Cronbach's alpha = 0.730–0.837; McDonald's omega = 0.744–0.838). A five-factor confirmatory model fit better than models combining the interaction constructs, combining the mediators, or placing all items on one factor, although its absolute fit and discriminant validity were only partly satisfactory (CFI = 0.870, TLI = 0.857, RMSEA = 0.064, SRMR = 0.056). Regression estimates used HC3 robust standard errors, and indirect associations used 5,000 percentile-bootstrap samples. Parasocial interaction uniquely predicted community identification and self-efficacy, and both variables were associated with customer value co-creation. The indirect associations of parasocial interaction through community identification ( B = 0.163, 95% CI [0.038, 0.303]) and self-efficacy ( B = 0.167, 95% CI [0.053, 0.281]) were statistically detectable. Interpersonal interaction retained a direct association with customer value co-creation but did not uniquely predict either proposed mediator when both interaction variables were included; its two specific indirect associations were not statistically detectable. Results were similar after excluding uniform responders and after adding demographic and community-use controls. The findings distinguish relational and capability-related correlates of parasocial interaction while showing that interpersonal interaction may share substantial variance with brand-side relational experience. Because the data are cross-sectional, same-source, and affected by incomplete discriminant validity, the indirect effects are interpreted as covariance patterns consistent with the proposed pathways rather than evidence of causal psychological mechanisms.

item.title: When AI advice agrees or disagrees with human judgment: trust, self-efficacy, psychological resilience, and adaptive responses in physical education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
As AI-based decision-support systems become increasingly embedded in physical education and coaching practice, agreement and disagreement between algorithmic advice and participants’ immediate scenario judgments have become important but theoretically underexamined features of human-AI collaboration. Grounded in a shared Judge-Advisor System paradigm, four scenario-based experiments (total N = 859) manipulated whether an experimentally presented AI recommendation was consistent or conflicting with each participant’s prior judgment and tested machine trust and collaborative decision-making self-efficacy as psychological pathways to self-reported collaborative adaptive responses. Psychological resilience and rationale provision were examined as study-specific boundary conditions. Conflict significantly reduced machine trust (Study 1, d = 1.061) and self-efficacy (Study 2, B = −0.687), and both measured mediators carried significant negative indirect associations with adaptive responses (Study 1, B = −0.428; Study 2, via trust B = −0.201, via self-efficacy B = −0.127). Psychological resilience attenuated the between-condition difference in self-efficacy in Study 3 (index of moderated mediation = 0.115). In Study 4, rationale provision moderated the condition-to-trust association, F (1, 239) = 11.348, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.045: the conflict effect was −0.811 in the black-box condition but −0.182 when a rationale was provided. The manipulation therefore concerns advice-judgment agreement rather than a direct experimental comparison of data-driven judgment with established experiential intuition. Because the scenarios did not establish objective recommendation accuracy, the moderation patterns are interpreted as changes in psychological response rather than as evidence that preserving trust or self-efficacy necessarily improves calibration, decision quality, or welfare.

item.title: Prompt specificity and iterative behaviour in text-to-music co-creation: a secondary analysis of interaction logs and a framework for perceived creative control
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence can lower barriers to musical creation while also shifting consequential decisions away from the user. Methods This study examines that tension through a secondary analysis of the published PAGURI interaction-log prompt corpus and develops a tentative framework for perceived creative control. The analysable corpus contained 304 text-to-music prompts from 24 participants. Musical specificity was operationalised as explicit instrument and technical-parameter markers; iterative continuity was measured with Jaccard similarity between consecutive prompts and checked against TF-IDF cosine similarity. To avoid pseudoreplication, group comparisons were conducted on participant-level summaries rather than treating 304 prompts as independent cases. Results Role-derived experience groups differed substantially in mean prompt specificity, H(2) = 10.25, p = 0.006, ε 2 = 0.39, and specificity density, H(2) = 11.52, p = 0.003, ε 2 = 0.45, but not in refinement rate, H(2) = 0.24, p = 0.888. At a descriptive Jaccard threshold of 0.20, 46.8% of consecutive pairs were refinements and 53.2% were restarts; because this classification was threshold-sensitive, continuous similarity remained the primary continuity measure. Prompt specificity did not increase systematically across the session: the mean within-person Spearman correlation was ρ = −0.06, and the distribution of participant-level correlations did not differ significantly from zero, W = 89.0, p = 0.374. Discussion These findings distinguish the explicit technical-musical information users encode in prompts from the sequential continuity of their prompting behaviour. The paper integrates task structure, system autonomy, model coverage, prior experience, self-efficacy, and psychological ownership into a testable framework for future music-education research. Given the small participant-level sample and role-derived grouping, the empirical findings are exploratory and require confirmation in larger, controlled studies.

item.title: Engagement or disengagement: understanding the emotional dynamics of EFL learners in GenAI-assisted writing from the sociocultural perspective
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has reshaped EFL writing education, yet the emotional dimensions of student engagement in GenAI-assisted writing remain underexplored. This longitudinal multiple-case study investigates how Chinese EFL learners' emotional engagement evolves during a GenAI-assisted college writing course and what factors drive this evolution. Methods Drawing on the sociocultural framework of L2 student engagement with written feedback, we traced the emotional trajectories of three focal students across three writing tasks (exposition, group feature article, and argumentation) within a 14-week course. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with stimulated recall, reflective reports, GenAI-student chatlogs, drafts, informal chats, and course syllabus, and analyzed via thematic analysis. Results Our findings reveal three qualitatively distinct trajectories: positive-resilient, characterized by sustained positive affect with temporary fluctuations; pragmatic-transformative, marked by a gradual shift from practical disengagement to critical engagement; and vulnerable-contingent, moving from moderate disengagement, through tentative peer-mediated improvement, to eventual breakdown and intensified disengagement. These trajectories were shaped by the dialectical interplay between individual factors (e.g., English proficiency, GenAI literacy, mindsets, beliefs, and emotion regulation) and environmental factors (GenAI-relevant task design, peer and teacher mediation, and institutional policies). Discussion The study extends the sociocultural framework by identifying English proficiency and GenAI literacy as critical developmental competencies, embedding GenAI-related factors across multiple environmental levels, and foregrounding emotional engagement as a dynamic, fluid state that interacts with behavioral and cognitive engagement over time. The findings challenge universalist claims about GenAI's uniform affective benefits and underscore the need for differentiated pedagogical approaches that attend to learners' diverse emotional needs in GenAI-mediated writing contexts.

item.title: GenAI literacy and perceived decision quality in e-commerce: the mediating role of perceived information overload and the moderating role of consumer involvement
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support product search, comparison, and evaluation in e-commerce. However, consumers differ in their ability to use and critically evaluate GenAI-generated information, which may shape their perceived information overload and decision outcomes. Grounded in Information Processing Theory, this study examines the association between GenAI literacy and perceived decision quality, the mediating role of perceived information overload, and the moderating role of consumer involvement. Data were collected through an online survey of 401 Chinese college students and analyzed using confirmatory factor analysis and bootstrapped mediation and moderation procedures. The results show that GenAI literacy is positively associated with perceived decision quality and negatively associated with perceived information overload. Perceived information overload is negatively associated with perceived decision quality and accounts for a significant indirect association between GenAI literacy and perceived decision quality. Consumer involvement further moderates the association between GenAI literacy and perceived information overload: the negative association is stronger at higher levels of involvement. These findings support an information-processing account in which consumers’ GenAI-related capabilities and motivational involvement jointly shape their perceptions of cognitive burden and decision quality. The study highlights the importance of strengthening consumers’ critical GenAI literacy and adapting AI-supported information presentation to different levels of consumer involvement.

item.title: How AI disclosure influences consumers' purchase intention toward AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion: the roles of perceived usefulness, perceived authenticity, and algorithm aversion
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background With the growing application of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in fashion design and cultural and creative industries, AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion has created new opportunities for the contemporary transformation of traditional culture. However, whether consumers are willing to accept such products and how AI disclosure influences their evaluations and purchase intentions remain unclear. Drawing on the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model, this study examines the mechanisms through which AI disclosure, design aesthetics, cultural identity, perceived usefulness, perceived authenticity, and algorithm aversion influence consumers' purchase intentions toward AI-generated Chinese ethnic-minority fashion. Methods A questionnaire survey combined with a scenario-based experiment was employed. Six AI-generated fashion illustrations derived from Tujia costume elements were developed and selected as stimulus materials. Participants were randomly assigned to either an AI disclosure group or a non-disclosure group. Data were collected through Tencent Questionnaire, yielding 410 valid responses. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Importance–Performance Map Analysis (IPMA) were employed to examine the structural relationships, mediating effects, moderating effects, and practical priorities for improvement. Results Design aesthetics and cultural identity influenced purchase intention through perceived usefulness and perceived authenticity, with perceived usefulness emerging as the strongest predictor of purchase intention. AI disclosure significantly reduced design aesthetics, cultural identity, perceived usefulness, and perceived authenticity. Algorithm aversion did not significantly moderate the relationship between perceived usefulness and purchase intention but significantly strengthened the positive effect of perceived authenticity on purchase intention. Conclusions This study reveals the multiple psychological pathways through which AI disclosure shapes consumers' evaluations of AI-generated ethnic cultural fashion. The findings further indicate that algorithm aversion alters the extent to which consumers rely on authenticity judgments when forming purchase intentions. This study extends the application of the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S–O–R) model to the context of AI-generated cultural products and provides practical implications for balancing AI transparency, cultural authenticity, and the practical value of products.

item.title: Source-only cross-year prediction of perceived AI capability with a theory-anchored, loss-specific two-stage model
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Understanding how developers judge AI's ability to handle complex tasks can help organizations monitor attitudes toward AI at work. Repeated surveys provide an opportunity to study these judgments, but models used across years must combine useful prediction with clear interpretation of the roles of trust and favorability toward AI. Adding work-related information or changing the prediction objective can alter the coefficients used to describe those relationships. This study examines whether these goals can be separated using Theory-Anchored Residual Surface learning (TARS). Methods We analyzed repeated cross-sectional data from the official 2024 and 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Surveys ( n = 22, 757 and 17, 021 employed professional developers). The outcome was respondents' five-category rating of how well AI tools handle complex development tasks. TARS first models its relationship with trust in output accuracy and favorability toward AI, then uses work and demographic information to correct prediction errors while keeping the first-stage coefficients fixed. Model development used 2024 data alone; 2025 outcomes were reserved for evaluation against models trained under the same protocol. Results In both surveys, higher trust and favorability were associated with higher perceived capability, with trust showing the stronger association. In the cross-year evaluation, TARS achieved R 2 = 0.445 (95% CI [0.434, 0.456]) and mean absolute error = 0.742. Changing the second-stage tuning objective improved absolute-error prediction while retaining the same first-stage coefficients. Discussion These findings show how repeated surveys can support prediction of perceived AI capability while keeping the reported trust-favorability relationship consistent across model adjustments. The approach offers an interpretable way to study professional appraisals of AI as work contexts and prediction priorities change.

item.title: Generative-augmented multimodal neuroaffective decoding for product evaluation: toward neurofeedback-driven human-in-the-loop co-design
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Background Kansei engineering traditionally relies on self-reported evaluations of product impressions, which are susceptible to contextual influences, recall bias, and assessment timing. Multimodal psychophysiological measurements offer complementary insights into affective responses, but integrating heterogeneous signals with limited sample sizes remains challenging. This study proposes Generative-Augmented Multimodal Affective Fusion (GAMAF) to predict perceived attractiveness, innovativeness, and friendliness in product evaluation. Methods GAMAF integrates feature-space conditional Wasserstein generative adversarial learning with gradient penalty (cWGAN-GP), cross-modal attention, graph-based interactions, and adaptive modality weighting. Fifty participants evaluated three automobile cockpit designs, yielding 150 participant–stimulus trials after multimodal quality control. Electroencephalography (EEG), eye tracking (ET), and peripheral physiological signals were integrated and evaluated using nested participant-wise cross-validation. Results GAMAF achieved mean outer-fold R² values of 0.810, 0.850, and 0.840 for attractiveness, innovativeness, and friendliness, respectively, each with a standard deviation of 0.016. These values exceeded those of the Multimodal Transformer baseline (0.75, 0.78, and 0.76, respectively). Across the three targets, GAMAF reduced aggregate mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE) by approximately 29.6% and 29.7%, respectively. Ablation analyses supported the integrated architecture, while adaptive modality weights revealed target-dependent patterns. Discussion GAMAF demonstrates the potential of generative-augmented multimodal fusion for decoding Kansei-related product impressions. However, performance comparisons remain descriptive because baseline variability and participant-level uncertainty were not quantified. Further validation on unseen product designs and closed-loop design optimization is needed to establish its generalizability and practical utility.

item.title: From a surgeon's stroke to a third hemisphere—The auxilium architecture for brain restoration and extension
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
A surgeon was exercising on a stationary bicycle when he had a large ischemic left middle cerebral artery territory stroke, complicated by hemorrhagic transformation requiring hemicraniectomy and cranioplasty. He developed right-sided spastic hemiplegia and a mixed aphasia. This paper takes that case as its anchor to pose the question: beyond improving residual function, what would it mean to restore cognitive function that was lost so that the person fully returns to their pre-stroke baseline? Existing brain-computer interfaces rely on the person having an intact cortical substrate for intended movement and speech. Here we propose the Auxilium, a brain restoration architecture for the situation where that substrate is no longer present: an extracranial auxiliary brain system, agnostic to its substrate, that connects to a person's residual cortex through whatever input-output technology proves most appropriate, and that supplies, in parallel and in real time, new substrate, whether biological or synthetic. We address an assumption of brain-computer interface development, that throughput is the binding constraint. Linking a kHz brain to MHz digital does not impart the higher clock speed, because the limitation lies not in the port but in the architecture of the entire brain and body imparted by evolution. We posit that the substrate of canonical circuits and their integration areas is essential, and the Auxilium can be understood as restoring both connectivity (linkage between disconnected areas) and computation (information generation capability of a volume of neural tissue). We propose a near-term de-risking pipeline using stereoelectroencephalography during surgical epilepsy evaluation, comparing extracranial modules spanning threshold rules, PID controllers, expert systems, artificial neural networks, neuromorphic devices, and biological specimens, each linked in real time to a participant serving as their own control on naturalistic tasks. If ports alone restore the lost function, the requirement is routing connectivity. If performance improves only when the module supplies its own dynamics, the requirement is computational substrate. We expect the answer to depend on how much tissue was lost, how quickly, and on the individual's reserve, and we treat routing and substrate as endpoints of a continuum to be mapped empirically.

item.title: Data-driven subgroups of adolescent depression: integrating EEG-derived brain networks, childhood trauma, and depressive symptoms
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Abstract Background Adolescent major depressive disorder (MDD) is characterized by marked clinical heterogeneity and heightened sensitivity to psychosocial adversity, particularly childhood trauma. Ongoing neurodevelopment and brain plasticity during adolescence may limit the applicability of adult-derived neurobiological models. Previous studies have rarely integrated large-scale network connectivity, trauma exposure, and symptom dimensions within a single multivariate framework and have largely relied on functional magnetic resonance imaging or univariate electroencephalographic (EEG) measures. Methods This cross-sectional case-control study included 67 medication-free adolescents with MDD and 35 matched healthy controls. Resting-state source-space EEG functional connectivity was estimated. Sparse canonical correlation analysis (sCCA) was used to identify multivariate associations between network connectivity and clinical and childhood-trauma measures. Moderation analysis examined whether network connectivity moderated the association between trauma and depression severity. K-means clustering of sCCA-derived canonical variates was used to identify data-driven patient subgroups. Results Adolescents with MDD showed lower default mode network (DMN)-limbic network (LMN) connectivity than healthy controls. The only sCCA mode meeting the prespecified robustness criteria linked physical abuse, emotional neglect, and anxiety/somatization to distributed connectivity features, particularly those involving the frontoparietal, limbic, visual, and salience networks. Within-visual-network connectivity moderated the association between childhood trauma and depression severity. Clustering identified two patient subgroups with distinct symptom and network profiles. Conclusions EEG-derived network measures may help characterize the interplay between childhood trauma and clinical heterogeneity in adolescent MDD. These preliminary findings require replication in larger, independent samples. Clinical trial number not applicable

item.title: When AI Enters the Pencil Box: A Longitudinal Study of Child–LLM Writing Collaboration in a Chinese Primary School
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
We report a qualitative study spanning more than six months with upper-primary students (ages 9–12) in southern China using a local LLM (Doubao) for writing. Two interview waves with ten students (nine re-interviewed) and six teachers (three re-interviewed) reveal a set of recurring shifts in our focal cohort: from novelty to strategy, from anthropomorphic “companion/virtual teacher” to tool-like framing, and from quick unsticking to guarded use shaped by dependence, fairness, and exam-transfer Footnote1 concerns. Students valued speed and breadth but noted mechanical tone, age/style mismatch, and weak transfer to AI-free tests. We map a Control × Dependency framework and before/after transitions, and surface tensions around classroom norms and equity amid policy ambiguity and uneven AI literacy. We suggest process-visible, agency-preserving integration: sentence- and phrase-level provenance with mandatory micro-edits, task-specific scaffold ceilingsFootnote2, and process-anchored assessment schemes that explicitly factor in AI-use traces.

item.title: Does Code-Switching Disrupt Emotion Recognition? A Valence–Arousal Analysis of Affective Misalignment in Multilingual Human–AI Interaction
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
As multilingual communication increasingly involves code-switching, emotion recognition in mixed-language input has become a key challenge for human–AI interaction. This study examines emotion classification under English–Spanish and Spanish–English code-switching conditions using the valence–arousal framework. Five large language models (GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-5, Llama-3, Llama-4, and Claude Opus 4.7) were evaluated on 7,560 inputs across five code-switching ratios. Performance was assessed using accuracy, Macro-F1, and mixed-effects logistic regression, while errors were categorized as valence shifts, arousal shifts, or same-region confusions. Increasing code-switching produced a small but significant accuracy decline in both language directions. Under English-to-Spanish conditions, models generally preserved valence while showing greater arousal instability. Under Spanish-to-English conditions, GPT-5 showed increased valence-shift errors and was the only model with a significant direction–error-type association. Aggregate metrics can obscure distinct forms of affective misalignment. The proposed framework enables dimension-level comparison of error patterns across models, language directions, and code-switching ratios.
